newsitem.title: SWEDEN: NATO CHIEF SAYS TALKS CONTINUING OVER RUSSIA PACT.
newsitem.headline: NATO CHIEF SAYS TALKS CONTINUING OVER RUSSIA PACT.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Wednesday ruled out any deal being signed this year on future relations between Russia and the western alliance.
"No formal signature will take place in 1996," Solana told a news conference during the first official visit of a NATO chief to neutral Sweden.

Solana was quoted by the Russian news agency Interfax on Tuesday as saying he hoped to sign a deal on future relations by the end of the year, but NATO officials travelling with Solana said the Russian report was incorrect.
Arriving in Stockholm for a brief visit, Solana said he saw talks with Russia over a planned document on future relations as part of a process which would culminate in mid-1997.
The plan by NATO to seal a charter with Russia is part of its eastward enlargement of the 16 member alliance that is due to be settled by 1999, the 50th anniversary of NATO.

It is universally acknowledged that Russia cannot be frozen out of a future pan-European security arrangement, and Moscow wants to strike a deal that will guarantee its interests in the post-expansion period.
Moscow has denounced NATO plans to expand to include the former Soviet bloc states in central and eastern Europe, saying an enlarged NATO could threaten Russia's national security.
But Solana said NATO negotiations over enlargement and the treaty with Russia were not intertwined.
"There is no relationship between the enlargement and bilateral relations with Russia," Solana said.

"We will not consider this process as a process of sequence. We consider this process a converging process. I would like to see these processes converging towards a summit that will take place in about a year."
Solana described NATO's relationship with Russia at present as good but said there was room for improvement.
"I think (relations) could be better," he added. "But we have participated together in Bosnia, we have good channels of communication.
"We do not agree on everything, that is why we keep on talking ... to see if we can overcome the difficulties."
Solana has earlier said the NATO-Russia document was expected to consist of three parts; a declaration, a mechanism for consultations and, thirdly, a mechanism for cooperation.
He said NATO was not a threat to Russia, but it was important to formalise bilateral relations.
"If NATO is not a threat to Russia today why should it be considered that an enlarged NATO is a threat to Russia tomorrow?" Solana said during a debate with Swedish politicians.
"We want to continue talking to them, to try to dispel misconceptions and I hope between now and 1997 we will be able to establish a profound, bilateral relationship with Russia."
